question: How large is the global mental-disorder burden, and where does treatment capacity lag behind need?

geographies: countries where official system-capacity data are available
research_scope.period: 2021 burden estimates; 2024 Mental Health Atlas survey; long-run trend target 1990-2023
research_scope.population: general population, with disorder-specific treatment populations where stated
exclusions: national wellbeing rankings inferred from modeled prevalence
causal claims not supported by source design
redistributing restricted IHME exports without checking the applicable data-use agreement

sources.license_note: WHO publication page states CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO for non-commercial reuse with attribution; commercial reuse requires permission.
sources.method_note: WHO synthesis using the latest available epidemiological evidence, including GBD 2021 estimates produced by IHME.

sources.title: Mental disorders
sources.license_note: Use WHO material with attribution and according to WHO reuse terms.

sources.license_note: WHO publication page states CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO for non-commercial reuse with attribution; commercial reuse requires permission.

sources.method_note: Public country-profile PDFs expose standardized fields for financing, workforce, governance and service capacity, but coverage is limited to responding countries.

sources.title: Global Health Metrics: Mental disorders—Level 2 cause (GBD 2021)
sources.publisher: Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation

sources.method_note: GBD 2021 modeled estimates with 95% uncertainty intervals; mental-disorder DALYs are overwhelmingly YLDs because fatal burden is only directly assigned to selected causes such as eating disorders.

claims.statement: An estimated 1.095 billion people were living with a mental disorder globally in 2021.
claims.locator: World mental health today, Table 2.1; WHO Mental disorders fact sheet, opening epidemiology section
claims.definition: Point prevalence of GBD 2021 mental-disorder categories, adjusted for independent comorbidity but not dependent comorbidity.
claims.method_note: Modeled estimate, not a count of diagnosed people. WHO rounds this to 1.1 billion / nearly one in seven in public-facing text.
claims.license_note: Use as an attributed numeric claim; do not imply the underlying microdata are WHO-owned or freely redistributable.
claims.verification_note: Cross-checked the exact 1,095 million value in WHO Table 2.1 against the WHO fact-sheet rounded figure of 1.1 billion.

claims.statement: The age-standardized prevalence of mental disorders was estimated at 13.6% globally in 2021.
claims.locator: Table 2.1
claims.definition: Age-standardized prevalence across the GBD 2021 mental-disorder aggregate.
claims.method_note: Use for global scale, not as a simple national wellbeing ranking metric.
claims.verification_note: Read directly from WHO Table 2.1 and checked against the report's nearly-one-in-seven framing.

claims.statement: Anxiety disorders affected an estimated 359 million people globally in 2021.
claims.locator: Table 2.1
claims.definition: WHO table notes that the GBD anxiety category includes anxiety disorders and PTSD.
claims.method_note: Modeled prevalence estimate.

claims.statement: Depressive disorders affected an estimated 332 million people globally in 2021.
claims.locator: Table 2.1
claims.definition: WHO table includes major depressive disorder and dysthymia in depressive disorders.
claims.method_note: Modeled prevalence estimate.

claims.statement: Mental disorders accounted for an estimated 155 million DALYs globally in 2021.
claims.locator: GBD 2021 Mental disorders Level 2 cause summary, opening summary
claims.definition: Disability-adjusted life years attributable to the GBD mental-disorders Level 2 cause.
claims.method_note: 95% uncertainty interval 117–198 million; the source says YLDs contributed to almost all mental-disorder DALYs.
claims.license_note: Use as an attributed result under applicable IHME terms.
claims.verification_note: Checked point estimate and uncertainty interval in the IHME GBD 2021 cause summary.

claims.statement: Mental disorders accounted for about 5.4% of global DALYs in 2021.
claims.locator: GBD 2021 Mental disorders Level 2 cause summary, opening summary
claims.definition: Share of all-cause DALYs attributed to mental disorders in GBD 2021.
claims.method_note: 95% uncertainty interval 4.3–6.5%.
claims.license_note: Use as an attributed result under applicable IHME terms.
claims.verification_note: Checked point estimate and uncertainty interval in the IHME GBD 2021 cause summary.

claims.definition: Income-group medians/range for specialized mental-health workers per 100,000 population.
claims.method_note: The report presents the low-income and lower-middle-income values as a 1.1–2.4 range in its summary; retain the range rather than collapsing it to one point estimate.

claims.statement: High-income countries reported a median 67.2 specialized mental-health workers per 100,000 people.
claims.locator: Executive summary, p. 3; financing and workforce
claims.definition: Income-group median specialized mental-health workforce per 100,000 population.
claims.method_note: Compare with low-income groups only as a health-system capacity indicator, not as a direct measure of care quality.

claims.statement: Fewer than 10% of responding countries had fully moved from institutional models to community-based mental-health care.
claims.locator: Executive summary, p. 3; mental health services
claims.definition: Countries assessed as fully transitioned from institutional-based to community-based service models.
claims.method_note: The source reports an inequality, not an exact percentage; retain 'fewer than 10%' in prose.

claims.statement: 52.9% of responding countries remained in an early stage of transition toward community-based mental-health care.
claims.locator: Executive summary, p. 3; mental health services
claims.definition: Countries classified in the Atlas as remaining in an early stage of service transition.
claims.method_note: A systems-reform indicator, not a patient-level outcome.

claims.statement: Psychosis service coverage was estimated at about 40% in the small set of countries with sufficiently complete data.
claims.population: People with psychosis in 22 countries with sufficient data
claims.locator: Table 34 / executive summary service coverage section
claims.definition: Estimated proportion of people with psychosis who received services, derived from treated prevalence divided by estimated psychosis prevalence.
claims.method_note: The Atlas explicitly says the estimate is indicative rather than definitive because only 22 countries provided sufficient data. Table 34 gives mean 41% and median 40%; use 40% as the report's summary figure.

claims.statement: A WHO fact sheet states that only 29% of people with psychosis receive formal mental-health care, citing Mental Health Atlas 2020.
claims.locator: Health systems and social support section
claims.definition: Formal mental-health care coverage for people with psychosis as summarized by WHO using Atlas 2020 evidence.
claims.method_note: Do not present this as a directly comparable predecessor to the Atlas 2024 40% estimate; coverage definitions, source years and country samples differ.

claims.period: Studies with data from 2000–2019; review published 2022

claims.statement: An estimated 12 billion productive work days are lost each year to depression and anxiety.
claims.period: Annual estimate cited in WHO 2025 report
claims.population: Working-age population; underlying study covered 36 countries representing about 80% of global population
claims.locator: Chapter 3, economic consequences, p. 29
claims.definition: Productive work days lost through absenteeism, presenteeism and staff turnover associated with depression and anxiety.
claims.method_note: WHO 2025 report cites a 2016 economic analysis; use as an economic framing estimate, not a current administrative count.
claims.license_note: WHO reuse terms apply; cite the underlying study when used prominently.

claims.statement: The same analysis estimated nearly US$1 trillion per year in productivity losses from depression and anxiety.
claims.period: Annual estimate cited in WHO 2025 report
claims.population: Working-age population; underlying study covered 36 countries representing about 80% of global population
claims.locator: Chapter 3, economic consequences, p. 29
claims.definition: Estimated productivity cost associated with depression and anxiety.
claims.method_note: Based on a 2016 analysis cited by WHO; useful for scale but not a contemporaneous 2025 accounting estimate.
claims.license_note: WHO reuse terms apply; cite the underlying study when used prominently.

conflicts.issue: Psychosis treatment/service coverage figures of 29% and about 40% should not be read as a trend.
conflicts.resolution: Keep both as separately scoped evidence. The 29% figure is a WHO fact-sheet synthesis citing Mental Health Atlas 2020; the ~40% Atlas 2024 figure is derived from only 22 countries with sufficient data and the report labels it indicative rather than definitive. Do not draw a 29→40 improvement line.

recommendations.action: Do not block version 1 on a giant IHME country export
recommendations.why: WHO 2025 already gives publishable global burden estimates, while WHO Atlas 2024 and GHO provide the strongest directly actionable evidence on financing, workforce and service capacity.

recommendations.action: Make the main story burden → capacity mismatch, not a prevalence league table
recommendations.why: Modeled prevalence is sensitive to case definitions, source coverage and modeling assumptions. Ranking countries by prevalence alone invites a false 'mentally healthier country' interpretation.

recommendations.action: Use WHO Atlas country profiles as the next extraction target
recommendations.why: They are public, standardized and directly aligned with the editorial question; a country-capacity map can be built without an IHME request.

recommendations.action: Treat psychosis service coverage and MDD treatment coverage as qualified evidence
recommendations.why: The psychosis estimate is based on only 22 countries and the depression meta-regression has sparse evidence from low-resource settings. These figures show a care gap but should not be over-precise.

recommendations.action: Keep counts, rates, budgets and workforce measures in separate visual grammars
recommendations.why: A billion-person count communicates scale; age-standardized prevalence supports comparison; budget share and workers per 100,000 describe capacity. Combining them into a single index would hide important semantics.

candidate_questions: A billion-person need, but how much treatment capacity does the world actually have?
Where are mental-health systems most constrained by workforce and financing?
Why does a global mental-health story look different when we measure disability and care capacity instead of deaths?
How far has the world moved from psychiatric institutions toward community-based mental-health care?
story_handoff.recommended_question: A billion people live with mental disorders. How unequal is the capacity to care for them?
caveats: GBD prevalence estimates are modeled estimates, not diagnosed-case registries or direct measures of subjective wellbeing.
Country-level mental-health system data have nonresponse and differing reference years; missing must never be encoded as zero.
Atlas medians describe responding countries and should not be presented as population-weighted global averages.
Psychosis service coverage in Atlas 2024 is based on only 22 countries and is explicitly described as indicative rather than definitive.
Treatment estimates from systematic reviews carry wide uncertainty intervals, especially in low-resource settings.
Do not compare the WHO fact-sheet 29% psychosis-care figure directly with the Atlas 2024 ~40% figure as a time trend.

executive_answer: The evidence is already strong enough to build the next version of the story without waiting for a massive IHME export. WHO's latest synthesis estimates 1.095 billion people living with mental disorders in 2021 (13.6% age-standardized prevalence), while GBD 2021 attributes about 155 million DALYs to mental disorders and says almost all of that burden is nonfatal disability. The system response is much thinner and highly unequal: Mental Health Atlas 2024 reports a global median of 2.1% of government health spending allocated to mental health and 13.5 specialized mental-health workers per 100,000 people, with only around 1.1–2.4 in low/lower-middle-income settings versus 67.2 in high-income settings. Treatment evidence shows the same gradient, but with important data limitations. The executable route is therefore to build country-level capacity visuals now from WHO GHO and Atlas country profiles, use published GBD estimates for the global burden framing, and treat an IHME country-level prevalence/YLD request as an optional enhancement rather than a blocker.
